title: Fractions: The Great Pizza Share
subject: Mathematics
instructions: A hand-authored demo lesson, used as the offline backup module.

blocks.narration: Open with a fair-share problem everyone has lived through.

data.text: Four friends. One big pizza. Nobody wants the smallest slice. How do we make the shares exactly fair?

blocks.narration: Name the two numbers and the job each one does.

data.heading: Meet the Numerator and Denominator
paragraphs: When we split a whole into equal parts, each part is a fraction of the whole.
The bottom number, the denominator, says how many equal pieces the whole was cut into. Cut the pizza into 4 equal slices and the denominator is 4.
The top number, the numerator, says how many of those pieces we took. Grab 3 of the 4 slices and you have 3/4 of the pizza.

blocks.narration: Place the quarters between 0 (no pizza) and 1 (whole pizza).

data.question: Tap each mark. Where does three quarters of the pizza land?

blocks.narration: Show that different names can be the same amount.

data.caption: All three bars fill the same length. These are equivalent fractions.

blocks.narration: A repeatable recipe for a fair share.

steps.title: Count the sharers
steps.text: How many people need a share? That count is your denominator.

steps.title: Cut equal pieces
steps.text: Split the whole into that many equal pieces. Equal is the whole point.

steps.title: Hand them out
steps.text: Give one piece to each sharer. Each person now holds one unit fraction.

steps.title: Name the share
steps.text: Write it: pieces you have on top, total pieces on the bottom.

blocks.narration: Check understanding with a fair, correct-by-construction question.

data.question: You cut a pizza into 8 equal slices and eat 2. How much of the pizza is left?
data.explanation: 8 slices total, 2 eaten, so 6 remain. That is 6 out of 8, or 6/8 (the same as 3/4).

blocks.narration: Hands-on proof that equal shares can look different.

data.title: Paper pizza share
instructions: Work in pairs. Each pair takes two paper circles of the same size.
Fold one circle into 2 equal parts and the other into 4 equal parts.
Shade 1 part of the first circle and 2 parts of the second circle.
Place them side by side. Are the shaded amounts the same?
Write what you found in one sentence.

questions: Draw a pizza cut into 4 equal parts and shade 3 of them. Write the fraction.
Give one fraction that means the same amount as 1/2.

points: Many children think 1/6 is bigger than 1/3 because 6 is bigger. Use the paper circles, not words.
Insist on the word 'equal' every time a part is named.
If time runs short, move the paper pizza share to homework.
